For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $H^*H=I_2$. Also $He_0=(e_0+e_1)/\sqrt2$, so $H$ is a unitary one-qubit operation in the specified basis.

By the tensor-map rule [F5], $H^{\otimes n}e_{0^n}=(He_0)^{\otimes n} =2^{-n/2}(e_0+e_1)^{\otimes n} =2^{-n/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}e_x.$ The last equality distributes the finite tensor product over its two-term factors, choosing exactly one of $e_0,e_1$ at each position; the ordered product basis in [F2] identifies these choices with the binary words $x$. For $n=0$, both sides are the scalar $1$ in $\mathbb C$, the empty sum-index set convention gives its single empty word, and [F5] makes the empty tensor map the identity. The basis vectors are distinct orthonormal vectors by [F3], so the right side has norm one.

By [F5], the construction applies one copy of $H$ to each of the $n$ tensor factors and no oracle operation. It therefore has $n$ one-qubit gate instances when $H$ is primitive, as counted by [F4]; if it is not primitive, the declared synthesis cost is required. At $n=0$ the circuit has no gates.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
normal, and write the spectral resolution from
[[thm-spectral-resolution-and-polynomial-spectral-projections]] as

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

where the $\lambda_j$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$ and $P_j$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$. For a function
$f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$ on the spectrum of $T$, define

$$f(T):=\sum_{j=1}^r f(\lambda_j)P_j.$$

This is the **spectral functional calculus** of $T$. For the identity function
$\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}$, one has $\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}(T)=T$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Fix $z\in\mathbb C$. Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set $\mathbb C$, the
initial value $1$, and the function $w\mapsto wz$. This defines the natural
powers uniquely by
$$ z^0=1,\qquad z^{n+1}=z^nz\quad(n\in\mathbb N). $$

Let $\jmath\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ be the embedding of
[[lem-nat-embeds-int]]. For an integer $r\ge0$, that lemma gives a unique
$n\in\mathbb N$ with $r=\jmath(n)$; define $z^r:=z^n$. If $r<0$ and $z\ne0$,
there is a unique $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $-r=\jmath(n)$; define
$$ z^r:=(z^n)^{-1}. $$
The inverse exists because $\mathbb C$ is a field by
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]. Thus nonnegative integer powers are
defined for every $z$, while negative integer powers are defined exactly when
$z\ne0$; in particular $0^0=1$ and no negative power of $0$ is defined. The
integer and its unique natural representative are never conflated.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

derivations.claim: If $Hv=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, then self-adjointness gives $\lambda\langle v,v\rangle=\langle Hv,v\rangle=\langle v,Hv\rangle =\overline\lambda\langle v,v\rangle$ by [F1]–[F3], so every eigenvalue $\lambda$ is real. Since $H$ is self-adjoint it is normal, and [F4] supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis. In dimension zero the assertions below hold for the unique endomorphism.

Write the spectral resolution $H=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$ over distinct eigenvalues. The projections satisfy $P_\lambda^*=P_\lambda$, $P_\lambda P_\mu=0$ for $\lambda\ne\mu$, and $\sum_\lambda P_\lambda=I_V$. Definition [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]] is the functional-calculus sum in [F5]. By [F11], at $z=0$ the exponential series has first term $1$ and every later term $0$, so every partial sum is $1$ and $e^0=1$.

The adjoint of this sum is $U_H(t)^*=\sum_\lambda e^{it\lambda}P_\lambda$. Thus $U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=\sum_\lambda |e^{-it\lambda}|^2P_\lambda =\sum_\lambda P_\lambda=I_V$, since $t\lambda$ is real and [F7] gives $|e^{-it\lambda}|=e^0=1$ by step 2.1. At $t=0$ every coefficient is $1$ by step 2.1, so $U_H(0)=I_V$.
The product $U_H(t)U_H(s)$ has coefficient $e^{-it\lambda}e^{-is\lambda}=e^{-i(t+s)\lambda}$ on each $P_\lambda$ by [F6]; all cross terms vanish by orthogonality. Hence $U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s)$.

For each real eigenvalue $\lambda$, the difference quotient of $t\mapsto e^{-it\lambda}$ at $t$ equals $e^{-it\lambda}(e^{-i\lambda h}-1)/h$ by [F6]. If $\lambda\ne0$, set $z=-i\lambda h$ and use [F8] at $0$, together with $e^0=1$ from step 2.1, to obtain the limit $-i\lambda e^{-it\lambda}$; if $\lambda=0$, the quotient is identically zero. The spectral sum is finite, so differentiating it term by term gives $U_H'(t)=\sum_\lambda(-i\lambda)e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda=-iHU_H(t)$.

Let $Y$ be any differentiable solution with $Y(0)=I_V$. Write its entries in the orthonormal eigenbasis from step 1.1 as $y_{jk}(t)$. Taking each matrix coordinate of the difference quotient for $Y'(t)=-iHY(t)$ gives $y_{jk}'(t)=-i\lambda_jy_{jk}(t)$. Put $q_j(t):=e^{i\lambda_jt}$. By [F6], for $h\ne0$, $$\frac{q_j(t+h)-q_j(t)}h=e^{i\lambda_jt}\frac{e^{i\lambda_jh}-1}h.$$ If $\lambda_j=0$, this quotient is zero. Otherwise set $z=i\lambda_jh$; [F8] at $0$, with $e^0=1$ from step 2.1, gives $\lim_{z\to0}(e^z-1)/z=1$, and hence $q_j'(t)=i\lambda_jq_j(t)$. The real and imaginary parts of $y_{jk}$ and $q_j$ are differentiable. Since $\operatorname{Re}(q_jy_{jk})=(\operatorname{Re}q_j)(\operatorname{Re}y_{jk})-(\operatorname{Im}q_j)(\operatorname{Im}y_{jk})$ and $\operatorname{Im}(q_jy_{jk})=(\operatorname{Re}q_j)(\operatorname{Im}y_{jk})+(\operatorname{Im}q_j)(\operatorname{Re}y_{jk})$, the real product rule [F10] gives the complex product rule. Thus $g_{jk}(t):=q_j(t)y_{jk}(t)$ is differentiable and $$g_{jk}'(t)=q_j'(t)y_{jk}(t)+q_j(t)y_{jk}'(t)=0.$$ Each real-valued component $h$ of $g_{jk}$ is therefore differentiable on $\mathbb R$ with derivative zero. It is continuous at every $c$: for $x\ne c$, $$h(x)-h(c)=\frac{h(x)-h(c)}{x-c}(x-c),$$ and the difference quotient tends to the finite value $h'(c)$, so it is bounded near $c$ and the product tends to zero. Thus both components are continuous on every $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Applying [F9] to each component on any $a<b$ shows both are constant on $\mathbb R$. Since $q_j(0)=1$ by step 2.1 and $Y(0)=I_V$, $g_{jk}(0)=\delta_{jk}$; therefore $y_{jk}(t)=\delta_{jk}e^{-i\lambda_jt}$ by [F6]. Thus $Y(t)=U_H(t)$. The zero-dimensional case has only one endomorphism and is unique as well.

Let $H$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex
inner-product space $V$. For real $t,s$, the evolution from
[[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]] satisfies
$$U_H(0)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s),\qquad \frac{d}{dt}U_H(t)=-iHU_H(t).$$
Moreover, $U_H$ is the unique differentiable map $Y:\mathbb R\to
\operatorname{End}(V)$ satisfying $Y'(t)=-iHY(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Two nonzero vectors $x,y\in H$ represent the same **ray** when $y=\alpha x$ for some nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb C$. A **pure state** is such a ray. If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite projective measurement on $H$. Then $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$ lies in $[0,1]$ for every $a$, and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let
$(e_y)_{y\in Y}$ be a finite orthonormal basis, and let $\phi\in V$ be a unit
vector. Measuring the pure state $[\phi]$ by the projective measurement onto
the basis lines outputs $y\in Y$ with probability
$$p_\phi(y)=|\langle \phi,e_y\rangle|^2,\qquad \sum_{y\in Y}p_\phi(y)=1.$$
In particular, for self-adjoint $H:V\to V$, real $t$, and unit $\psi$, the
walk output $\phi=U_H(t)\psi$ is unit and
$p_t(y)=|\langle U_H(t)\psi,e_y\rangle|^2$. For an initial vertex $e_x$, the
probability of observing vertex $y$ is $|\langle U_H(t)e_x,e_y\rangle|^2$.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Write $|w\rangle:=e_{\mathsf{enc}(w)}$ and $|r\rangle:=(N-1)^{-1/2}\sum_{x\ne w}e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}$. By [F4], [F12] these are orthonormal; the sum defining $|r\rangle$ has $N-1\ge1$ terms. In their ordered basis, [F1] gives $A|w\rangle=\sqrt{N-1}|r\rangle$ and $A|r\rangle=\sqrt{N-1}|w\rangle+(N-2)|r\rangle$. By [F5], $P_w|w\rangle=|w\rangle$ and $P_w|r\rangle=0$, so its restricted matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$. Thus their span $S$ is invariant under $H$, and the restricted matrices are $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sqrt{N-1}\\\sqrt{N-1}&N-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-\sqrt{N-1}/N\\-\sqrt{N-1}/N&-(N-2)/N\end{pmatrix}.$ In the full orthonormal computational basis [F12], $A$ has real symmetric entries between distinct encoded labels and zero entries elsewhere; [F5] makes $P_w$ diagonal with a single $1$. Hence the matrix of $H=-A/N-P_w$ is real symmetric, so $\langle Hx,y\rangle=\langle x,Hy\rangle$ for all $x,y$ and [F11] gives $H=H^*$. For $z\in S^\perp$ and $v\in S$, self-adjointness and invariance of $S$ give $\langle Hz,v\rangle=\langle z,Hv\rangle=0$, so $S^\perp$ is invariant too. Thus $H$ splits into self-adjoint blocks on $S$ and $S^\perp$. The input state is $|s\rangle=N^{-1/2}|w\rangle+\sqrt{(N-1)/N}|r\rangle$, which is unit because $|w\rangle,|r\rangle$ are orthonormal and the squared coefficients sum to $1$.

On this two-dimensional invariant span put $K:=H+(N-1)I/N$. Then $K=\frac1N\begin{pmatrix}-1&-\sqrt{N-1}\\-\sqrt{N-1}&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad K^2=I/N,\qquad \sqrt N K|s\rangle=-|w\rangle.$ The first two equalities follow by direct multiplication; for the last, the first coordinate of $K|s\rangle$ is $-1/\sqrt N$ and the second is $0$.

Let $P_\pm=(I\pm\sqrt N K)/2$. Step 2.1 and self-adjointness of $K$ give $P_\pm^2=P_\pm=P_\pm^*$, $P_+P_-=0$, $P_++P_-=I$, and $KP_\pm=\pm P_\pm/\sqrt N$. By step 1.1, each eigenspace of $H$ is the orthogonal sum of the corresponding eigenspaces of its two blocks: projecting $Hz=\lambda z$ onto either invariant summand preserves that equation. Therefore the spectral sum [F2] restricts on $S$ to the sum determined by $P_\pm$. On $S$, $H=K-(N-1)I/N$, so [F2] and [F6] give, for $a=t/\sqrt N$, $U_H(t)|_{S}=e^{it(N-1)/N}(e^{-ia}P_++e^{ia}P_-)$. citations.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex register and let $H=H^*$ be its
declared generator. The mathematical target at time $t\in\mathbb R$ is
$U_H(t)$ from [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]]. A **Hamiltonian-access
contract** records how this target and its input data are supplied; it does
not equate a matrix description with an implementation.

The contract declares one input representation:

1. **Explicit terms:** a finite ordered list of Hermitian matrices
   $H_1,\ldots,H_m$, real coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with their exact or
   finite-precision binary encodings, and the identity $H=\sum_{j=1}^m c_jH_j$.
   If the implementation calls the individual operations
   $U_{c_jH_j}(t_j)$, the contract lists every operation, its order, and its
   charge. The equality of their composition with $U_H(t)$ must be proved or
   supplied as a separate simulation certificate; it does not follow from the
   term list alone.
2. **Row-sparse input:** an integer sparsity bound $d$, a row-location oracle,
   and an entry-value oracle returning each selected matrix entry to a declared
   coefficient precision. Each oracle's full unitary action on invalid
   encodings, and every forward, inverse, or controlled call actually used, are
   explicit parts of the contract.

The contract separately names an implementation of the requested evolution:

- an ideal continuous-time operation $U_H(t)$ with its declared evolution
  time and/or evolution-query charge; or
- a finite unitary circuit/simulator $V_{H,t,\epsilon}$ with a supplied
  certificate $\|V_{H,t,\epsilon}-U_H(t)\|_{\rm op}\le\epsilon$ and its gate,
  query, description-bit, coefficient-precision, and classical-construction
  costs.

Initial-state preparation and final measurement are separate supplied stages.
For each stage the contract records a triple $(q,g,b)$: $q$ is the number of
declared oracle or evolution calls, $g$ is the finite gate count in the chosen
gate model, and $b$ is the declared input, operation-description, coefficient,
and precision-bit charge. Circuit description length and gate count follow
[[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]; they are distinct coordinates. Evolution time is
reported separately unless the chosen model explicitly includes it in a query
coordinate. Serial composition adds the declared stage coordinates. A
controlled or inverse operation is charged only if the model explicitly grants
that access or supplies a construction, as in
[[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and
[[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]].

A complexity claim for a family of such inputs must also specify a uniform
generator for the full circuit and access descriptions, as in
[[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and state the costs as functions of the
input size. The matrix alone supplies no efficient $U_H(t)$, controlled call,
inverse call, or zero-cost operation. In particular, a Boolean marked-item
oracle does not by itself grant the continuous-time operation
$e^{-it|e_w\rangle\langle e_w|}$; any conversion or simulation and its
precision are separately specified and charged.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

**Input:** An integer $n\ge0$, an ordered $n$-qubit register initialized to
$e_{0^n}$, and a Hamiltonian-access contract for
$$A_n:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}X_j,$$
where $X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$X_j:=I_2^{\otimes j}\otimes X\otimes I_2^{\otimes(n-j-1)}$ is its tensor-map
extension acting on factor $j$ and as the identity on every other factor, by
[[def-qc-tensor-map]]. The contract must explicitly
supply either the whole operation $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ or the $n$ local operations
$U_{X_j}(\pi/2)$ in the declared ordered tensor factors. The local-operation option requests each one-qubit evolution separately; its
equivalence to the whole evolution is proved by the correctness argument and
is not assumed here. This contract does not make arbitrary matrix exponentiation free. Every supplied query, gate, description-bit,
and synthesis cost is recorded under
[[def-qa-19-hamiltonian-access-cost-model]] and
[[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]].

**Procedure:** If the whole operation is supplied, apply $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ once.
If the local operations are supplied, apply $U_{X_j}(\pi/2)$ once for each
$j=0,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order. Then perform the computational-basis
projective measurement and return the observed $n$-bit word. For $n=0$, the
sum is empty, the register is the one-dimensional empty tensor product, the
evolution is the identity, and the output word is empty. For every $n$, the
operation and readout costs come from the declared access and circuit models;
the matrix formula alone supplies no implementation or cost.

For every integer $n\ge0$, the algorithm
[[alg-qa-19-hypercube-state-transfer]] evolves the initial vector $e_{0^n}$
to
$$U_{A_n}(\pi/2)e_{0^n}=(-i)^n e_{1^n}.$$
Consequently its computational-basis measurement outputs $1^n$ with
probability one, including the empty word when $n=0$.

**Inputs:** An integer $N\ge2$, an integer $m\ge\lceil\log_2N\rceil$, an
injective label encoding $\mathsf{enc}:[N]\to\{0,1\}^m$, and the corresponding
$m$-qubit register. Its **active subspace** is
$S:=\operatorname{span}\{e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}:x\in[N]\}$; bit strings outside the
image of $\mathsf{enc}$ are unused labels. The marked label $w\in[N]$ is available
through the declared oracle/access model, not as an inspected classical value.

On $S$, define the complete-graph adjacency by
$$A e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}:=\sum_{y\in[N],\,y\ne x}e_{\mathsf{enc}(y)},$$
and extend $A$ by zero on $S^\perp$. Define
$P_wz:=\langle z,e_{\mathsf{enc}(w)}\rangle e_{\mathsf{enc}(w)}$ on the full register and
the self-adjoint generator $H:=-A/N-P_w$.

The input also supplies:

- a state-preparation circuit $A_s$ whose label-register output from the
  specified zero input is the pure state
  $e_s:=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in[N]}e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}$; if its implementation uses
  workspace, the model states its initialization, final state, and separate
  query, gate, and description-bit costs;
- the total Boolean function $f_w:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}$ defined by
  $f_w(\mathsf{enc}(x))=1$ exactly when $x=w$ and $f_w(z)=0$ on every unused label,
  together with the full unitary XOR-oracle access and its cost from
  [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]]; and
- a Hamiltonian-access contract that supplies either the ideal $U_H(t)$ or a
  unitary simulator $V_{H,t,\rho}$ with a supplied certificate
  $\|V_{H,t,\rho}-U_H(t)\|_{\rm op}\le\rho$, including all query, gate,
  description-bit, precision, and classical-construction costs.

The function oracle does not itself supply the continuous-time operation
$U_H(t)$: any conversion from its marked predicate to evolution under $P_w$,
and any simulation of the adjacency term, must be separately declared and
charged under [[def-qa-19-hamiltonian-access-cost-model]].

**Procedure:** Prepare $e_s$, apply the supplied ideal evolution or simulator
for $t=\pi\sqrt N/2$, and measure the register in its computational basis
using [[def-qc-projective-measurement]]. Decode a measured string in the image
of $\mathsf{enc}$ to its label and return it; return `FAIL` on an unused string. If
$N=2^n$ and $\mathsf{enc}$ is the standard $n$-bit encoding, the supplied preparation
may be $A_s=H^{\otimes n}$ by
[[lem-qa-19-hadamard-uniform-state-preparation]]; charge $n$ gates when $H$
is primitive and the declared synthesis costs otherwise. For arbitrary $N$,
$A_s$ is a supplied, charged input. No query, gate, or runtime bound follows from
the finite matrix description alone.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

For an integer $n\ge0$, give each factor of the ordered register
$V_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}$ the basis $(e_0,e_1)$ and define the
one-qubit matrix
$$H:=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $H$ is unitary and
$$H^{\otimes n}e_{0^n}=2^{-n/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}e_x.$$
For $n=0$, the tensor product is $\mathbb C$, the empty word is the sole
basis label, and $H^{\otimes0}$ is the identity. The preparation uses exactly
$n$ one-qubit $H$ gates when $H$ is primitive in the declared circuit model;
otherwise its implementation and synthesis costs must be supplied there.

derivations.claim: Serial execution places the preparation, evolution, and readout costs in sequence. By the serial-composition rule [F1], each of the three coordinates is the sum of its corresponding stage coordinates; the finite gate and oracle coordinates remain separate as required by [F2].

In the hypercube instance, [F3] says the initial register is already $|0^n\rangle$, so no preparation gates are applied. If the procedure takes the local-operation branch, [F4] gives one one-qubit evolution operation for each of the $n$ tensor factors, hence $n$ local calls and $n$ gates exactly when those operations are primitive in the chosen gate model. If it takes the whole-operation branch, it calls the supplied $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ once and its contract declares that call's resource cost. The factorization theorem [F4] is an operator identity and does not turn a whole-operation call into $n$ calls. In either branch, measurement acts on the $n$ register wires, so its output word has $n$ bits by [F6].

In the complete-graph procedure, [F5] supplies a preparation with cost $C_s$, and the declared Hamiltonian and readout stages contribute their specified triples. Step 1.1 adds these triples; for $N=2^n$, [F7] verifies the standard-binary preparation with $n$ Hadamard gates (and zero oracle calls for that gate-only preparation). The measured encoding has $m$ bits by [F6]; classical decoding is charged separately. No preparation or simulation cost is inferred from $H$ itself.

Let $V$ be a finite vertex set with a fixed order and let
$w:V\times V\to[0,\infty)$ be symmetric. Self-loops are allowed and their
weight is counted once in each row sum. On $\mathbb C^V$ with ordered basis
$(e_v)_{v\in V}$, define the weighted adjacency matrix by
$A_{uv}=w(u,v)$, the degree $d(v)=\sum_{u\in V}w(v,u)$, and
$D_{vv}=d(v)$ with all off-diagonal entries zero. The **positive Laplacian**
is $L_+=D-A$; the other common sign convention is $L_-=A-D=-L_+$. A walk
generator records the chosen edge weights, loop convention, basis order, and
one of these signs. It is not a discrete transition matrix.

When every $d(v)>0$, the **normalized adjacency** is the separately defined
matrix $A_{\rm norm}=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$. No normalized-adjacency operation is
defined here at zero-degree vertices. The matrices $A,D,L_+,L_-$ are Hermitian:
$A_{vu}=w(v,u)=w(u,v)=\overline{A_{uv}}$ and $D$ is real diagonal. Under
the positive-degree condition, $D^{-1/2}$ is also real diagonal, so
$A_{\rm norm}^*=A_{\rm norm}$. A zero-vertex graph gives the zero coordinate
space and empty matrices; a quantum-walk input separately requires a
normalized state, so it has no instance on that space.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $(\varepsilon_k)$ be the alternating sequence of [[lem-alternating-sequence]],
that is the unique sequence of reals with $\varepsilon_0 = 1$ and
$\varepsilon_{k+1} = -\varepsilon_k$, which is what is usually written
$\varepsilon_k = (-1)^k$; let $e$ and $o$ be its even and odd index maps, so that
$\varepsilon_{e_j} = 1$, $\varepsilon_{o_j} = -1$, and every natural number is
$e_j$ for exactly one $j$ or $o_j$ for exactly one $j$.

Let $(b_k)$ be a sequence of reals that is nonincreasing
([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]); then
$b_k \ge 0$ for every $k$. Write $t_n := \sum_{k<n} \varepsilon_k b_k$ for the
partial sums ([[def-series]]). Then:

1. the series $\sum \varepsilon_k b_k$ converges; write $L$ for its sum;
2. $t_{e_j} \le L \le t_{o_j}$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, and for every
   $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the sum $L$ lies between the two consecutive partial sums
   $t_n$ and $t_{n+1}$;
3. $|L - t_n| \le b_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Claim 3 is the error bound: the partial sum $t_n$, which uses the $n$ terms
$\varepsilon_0 b_0, \dots, \varepsilon_{n-1}b_{n-1}$, differs from the sum by at
most the first term omitted.

**Only claim 1 is a corollary of [[thm-dirichlet-test]].** Claims 2 and 3 are not:
they come from the interlacing of the even-index and odd-index partial sums, and
that argument is carried out below rather than smuggled into the Dirichlet
estimate, which produces no bracketing at all.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $V$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let
$(e_y)_{y\in Y}$ be a finite orthonormal basis, and let $\phi\in V$ be a unit
vector. Measuring the pure state $[\phi]$ by the projective measurement onto
the basis lines outputs $y\in Y$ with probability
$$p_\phi(y)=|\langle \phi,e_y\rangle|^2,\qquad \sum_{y\in Y}p_\phi(y)=1.$$
In particular, for self-adjoint $H:V\to V$, real $t$, and unit $\psi$, the
walk output $\phi=U_H(t)\psi$ is unit and
$p_t(y)=|\langle U_H(t)\psi,e_y\rangle|^2$. For an initial vertex $e_x$, the

derivations.claim: For the two-vertex graph with one edge, in basis $(e_0,e_1)$ the adjacency swaps the basis vectors, $Ae_0=e_1$ and $Ae_1=e_0$, and $D=I$. Thus $L_+=I-A$, $L_-=-L_+$, and $A_{\rm norm}=A$. Put $u_+=(e_0+e_1)/\sqrt2$, $u_-=(e_0-e_1)/\sqrt2$, and $\psi=(e_0+i e_1)/\sqrt2$. Direct inner-product calculations using [F9] give $\|u_+\|=\|u_-\|=\|\psi\|=1$ and $\langle u_+,u_-\rangle=0$; direct application of $A$ gives $Au_+=u_+$ and $Au_-=-u_-$. Thus $(u_+,u_-)$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis.

For the three-vertex path with ordered vertices $0,1,2$, the degrees are $(1,2,1)$ and $Ae_0=e_1$, $Ae_1=e_0+e_2$, $Ae_2=e_1$. Thus $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad D=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{\rm norm}=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}=A/\sqrt2,\quad L_+=D-A,\quad L_-=A-D=-L_+.$ All degrees are positive, so [F1] defines $A_{\rm norm}$. Put $u_0=(e_0-e_2)/\sqrt2$, $u_+=(e_0+\sqrt2e_1+e_2)/2$, and $u_-=(e_0-\sqrt2e_1+e_2)/2$. By direct coordinate inner products in the standard orthonormal basis [F9], $(u_0,u_+,u_-)$ is an orthonormal basis; direct multiplication gives $Au_0=0$, $Au_+=\sqrt2u_+$, and $Au_-=-\sqrt2u_-$. The vectors $c=(e_0+e_1+e_2)/\sqrt3$, $u_0$, and $v=(e_0-2e_1+e_2)/\sqrt6$ also have unit norm and pairwise zero inner products. Direct multiplication gives $L_+c=0$, $L_+u_0=u_0$, and $L_+v=3v$. Hence the four generator spectra are $\sigma(A)=\{0,\pm\sqrt2\}$, $\sigma(A_{\rm norm})=\{0,\pm1\}$, $\sigma(L_+)=\{0,1,3\}$, and $\sigma(L_-)=\{0,-1,-3\}$. This directly compares adjacency, normalized adjacency, and both Laplacian signs on the irregular graph.

The spectral definition [F2] gives eigenphases $1,e^{-2i}$ for $U_{L_+}(1)$ on $(u_+,u_-)$ and $1,e^{2i}$ for $U_{L_-}(1)$. By [F3]–[F4], these are equivalently $e^{-i}(\cos1\,I+i\sin1\,A)$ and $e^{i}(\cos1\,I-i\sin1\,A)$: on $u_+$ and $u_-$, respectively, the coefficients are $1,e^{-2i}$ and $1,e^{2i}$. The $e_1$ coordinate after $U_{L_+}(1)$ is $e^{-i}i(\cos1+\sin1)/\sqrt2$; after $U_{L_-}(1)$ it is $e^{i}i(\cos1-\sin1)/\sqrt2$. Thus [F10] gives $p_+(1)=(\cos1+\sin1)^2/2$ and $p_-(1)=(\cos1-\sin1)^2/2$.

Put $\xi=(u_0+u_+)/\sqrt2$, which is unit by step 1.2, and fix the target ray $[\zeta]:=[U_A(\pi/\sqrt2)\xi]=[(u_0-u_+)/\sqrt2]$, since $e^{-i\pi}=-1$ by [F4], [F7]. For any real $t$, $U_A(t)\xi=(u_0+e^{-i\sqrt2t}u_+)/\sqrt2$ and $U_{A_{\rm norm}}(t)\xi=(u_0+e^{-it}u_+)/\sqrt2$ by [F1]–[F2]. Since the $u_0$ coefficient is the same nonzero number in both target and output, equality of rays forces the scalar multiple to be $1$ and is equivalent to equality of the displayed relative phases.

At $1$, the cosine-series magnitudes $b_k=1/(2k)!$ and sine-series magnitudes $c_k=1/(2k+1)!$ decrease to zero: each next factorial multiplies the denominator by a factor at least $2$, so both sequences tend to zero. By [F5]–[F6], the cosine sum lies above its two-term partial sum $1-1/2=1/2$, and the sine sum lies above $1-1/6=5/6$. Therefore $p_+(1)-p_-(1)=2\sin1\cos1\ge5/6>0$. The two Laplacian signs give different same-time measurement laws.

If $[U_A(t)\xi]=[\zeta]$, then $e^{-i(\sqrt2t-\pi)}=1$. By [F3]–[F4], this forces $\sin(\sqrt2t-\pi)=0$ and $\cos(\sqrt2t-\pi)=1$; [F8] puts the angle at $k\pi$, and [F7] shows $k$ must be even. Thus $t=\pi/\sqrt2+k\sqrt2\pi$. For $k\ge0$ this is at least $\pi/\sqrt2$; for $k\le-1$ it is at most $\pi/\sqrt2-\sqrt2\pi<0$. Hence its least nonnegative value is $\pi/\sqrt2$. The same argument for $A_{\rm norm}$ gives $t=\pi+2k\pi$, whose least nonnegative value is $\pi$. For the second family, $k=0$ gives $t=\pi$, every $k\ge1$ gives a larger time, and every $k\le-1$ gives a negative time. Thus the least nonnegative time is $\pi$. These runtimes differ because $\sqrt2>1$.

**Input:** An integer $n\ge0$, an ordered $n$-qubit register initialized to
$e_{0^n}$, and a Hamiltonian-access contract for
$$A_n:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}X_j,$$
where $X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$X_j:=I_2^{\otimes j}\otimes X\otimes I_2^{\otimes(n-j-1)}$ is its tensor-map
extension acting on factor $j$ and as the identity on every other factor, by
[[def-qc-tensor-map]]. The contract must explicitly
supply either the whole operation $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ or the $n$ local operations
$U_{X_j}(\pi/2)$ in the declared ordered tensor factors. The local-operation option requests each one-qubit evolution separately; its
equivalence to the whole evolution is proved by the correctness argument and
is not assumed here. This contract does not make arbitrary matrix exponentiation free. Every supplied query, gate, description-bit,
and synthesis cost is recorded under
[[def-qa-19-hamiltonian-access-cost-model]] and
[[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]].

**Procedure:** If the whole operation is supplied, apply $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ once.
If the local operations are supplied, apply $U_{X_j}(\pi/2)$ once for each
$j=0,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order. Then perform the computational-basis
projective measurement and return the observed $n$-bit word. For $n=0$, the
sum is empty, the register is the one-dimensional empty tensor product, the
evolution is the identity, and the output word is empty. For every $n$, the
operation and readout costs come from the declared access and circuit models;
the matrix formula alone supplies no implementation or cost.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $V$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let
$(e_y)_{y\in Y}$ be a finite orthonormal basis, and let $\phi\in V$ be a unit
vector. Measuring the pure state $[\phi]$ by the projective measurement onto
the basis lines outputs $y\in Y$ with probability
$$p_\phi(y)=|\langle \phi,e_y\rangle|^2,\qquad \sum_{y\in Y}p_\phi(y)=1.$$
In particular, for self-adjoint $H:V\to V$, real $t$, and unit $\psi$, the
walk output $\phi=U_H(t)\psi$ is unit and
$p_t(y)=|\langle U_H(t)\psi,e_y\rangle|^2$. For an initial vertex $e_x$, the
probability of observing vertex $y$ is $|\langle U_H(t)e_x,e_y\rangle|^2$.

For every integer $n\ge0$, the algorithm
[[alg-qa-19-hypercube-state-transfer]] evolves the initial vector $e_{0^n}$
to
$$U_{A_n}(\pi/2)e_{0^n}=(-i)^n e_{1^n}.$$
Consequently its computational-basis measurement outputs $1^n$ with
probability one, including the empty word when $n=0$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

By [F5], $U_X(t)$ acts on these vectors by $e^{-it}$ and $e^{it}$. On $f_+$, $\cos t\,I-i\sin t\,X$ acts by $\cos t-i\sin t=e^{-it}$; on $f_-$ it acts by $\cos t+i\sin t=e^{it}$, using [F6]–[F7]. Thus the two maps agree on a basis. At $t=\pi/2$, [F8] yields $U_X(\pi/2)=-iX$, so $U_X(\pi/2)e_0=-i e_1$.

The displayed matrix for $A_2$ follows by applying $X\otimes I+I\otimes X$ to each of the four basis vectors in [F2] using the tensor-map action [F11]. The four vectors $f_+\otimes f_+$, $f_+\otimes f_-$, $f_-\otimes f_+$, and $f_-\otimes f_-$ form a basis by [F2]–[F3]. On $f_\epsilon\otimes f_\eta$ with $\epsilon,\eta\in\{1,-1\}$, $A_2$ has eigenvalue $\epsilon+\eta$; [F5]–[F6] give evolution coefficient $e^{-i\pi(\epsilon+\eta)/2}=e^{-i\pi\epsilon/2}e^{-i\pi\eta/2}$, which is exactly the coefficient of $U_X(\pi/2)\otimes U_X(\pi/2)$ by [F11]. The operators therefore agree on a basis, and step 1.1 gives $U_{A_2}(\pi/2)=-X\otimes X$. Hence $U_{A_2}(\pi/2)e_{00}=-e_{11}$.

In the $n=1$ case, step 1.1 gives outcome $1$ amplitude $-i$; in the $n=2$ case, step 2.1 gives outcome $11$ amplitude $-1$. Both have squared modulus $1$, so [F9] gives the opposite-corner outcome with probability one in each case. These calculations are the $n=1,2$ instances of [F10].
